propositions.text: If returned to Turkey, appellant will be persecuted for political opinion (HDP membership) and religion (Alevi Muslim).
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) claims that if returned to Turkey, his country of nationality, he will be persecuted based on his political opinion (membership in the HDP (People's Democratic Party)) and his religion (Alevi Muslim).

propositions.text: RPD refused refugee protection on July 14, 2017, finding appellant lacked credibility and was excluded under Article 1E as permanent resident of Germany.
propositions.quote: His claim for refugee protection was refused by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on July 14, 2017 based on a finding that he lacked credibility and was excluded under Article 1E of the Geneva Convention,1 as he was a permanent resident of Germany.

propositions.text: Appellant now appeals to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).
propositions.quote: He now appeals to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

paragraphs.summary: Applicant claims persecution in Turkey for political and religious reasons; RPD refused protection for lack of credibility and Article 1E exclusion; appellant appeals to RAD.

propositions.text: Confirms RPD decision that appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection; appeal dismissed.
propositions.quote: I confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The appeal is dismissed.

propositions.text: Decision made pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of IRPA.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),

paragraphs.summary: Court confirms RPD decision denying refugee status and dismisses appeal under IRPA paragraph 111(1)(a).

propositions.text: Appellant claims membership in Kurdish party (HDP) and Alevi organizations, detained and tortured in Turkey for political activities.
propositions.quote: The Appellant claims to be a member of the "Kurdish party (HDP) and Alevi organizations (Pir Sultan Abdal association)." As a result of his political activities, he claims that he was detained, interrogated and tortured by the Turkish authorities.

propositions.text: Appellant applied for Canadian visa via agent/smuggler, who claimed appellant resided and worked in Germany.
propositions.quote: Through the use of an agent/smuggler,2 the Appellant applied for a Canadian visa, which was issued on XXXX XXXX, 2016. In support of the visa application, his agent/smuggler claimed that the Appellant resided in Germany and worked for a German company.

propositions.text: Documents submitted included passport, German residency card, banking documents, and employment letter from German company.
propositions.quote: A number of documents were submitted, including the Appellant's passport, a German Residency card (said to have been issued by the authorities in XXXX, Germany), banking documents indicating that the Appellant resided in Berlin and a letter from a German company confirming the Appellant's employment.

propositions.text: Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017 and made inland refugee claim on March 27, 2017.
propositions.quote: The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2017. He made an inland claim for refugee status on March 27, 2017.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant claims HDP and Alevi membership, tortured in Turkey; applied for Canadian visa via agent claiming German residence; submitted documents; arrived in Canada and claimed refugee status.

propositions.text: Appellant requests admission of two new documents at appeal: German Consulate letter and affidavit from friend Mr. XXXX.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has requested the admission of two documents at appeal: i) a letter from the German Consulate in Toronto indicating that the authorities in XXXX "confirmed that there is no registration of a person named XXXX XXXX XXXX, DOB: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Citizenship; TURKEY" and ii) an affidavit from a friend of the Appellant, a Mr. XXXX, dated September 25, 2017, outlining the Appellant's political activities in Turkey and in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant requests admission of German Consulate letter and affidavit from friend Mr. XXXX at appeal.

propositions.text: Subsection 110(4) IRPA limits new evidence admission to evidence arising after RPD rejection, not reasonably available then, or not reasonably expected to be presented then.
propositions.quote: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA limits the admission of evidence in an appeal before the RAD to evidence that: 1) arose after the RPD's rejection of the claim; 2) was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim; or 3) an Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim.

propositions.text: RAD rule 3(3)(g)(iii) requires detailed submissions on how new evidence meets subsection 110(4) and relates to appellant.
propositions.quote: RAD rule 3(3)(g)(iii) provides that an Appellant seeking the admission of new evidence must provide full and detailed submissions regarding how the evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellant.

propositions.text: If new evidence admissible under 110(4), must consider Singh factors: newness, credibility, relevance.
propositions.quote: If I find that the new evidence is admissible under subsection 110(4), I must then consider whether the evidence meets the factors elaborated by the Federal Court of Appeal in the Singh case, i.e. newness, credibility and relevance.

propositions.text: Threshold for admitting new evidence before RAD is high.
propositions.quote: The threshold for the admission of new evidence before the RAD is high.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains legal test for admitting new evidence on appeal under IRPA and RAD rules, including Singh factors and high threshold.

propositions.text: Appellant offers no explanation why German Consulate letter was not obtained before RPD rejection.
propositions.quote: As to the letter from the German Consulate, the Appellant does not offer an explanation as to why he could not have obtained this letter before the RPD's rejection of his claim.

propositions.text: Affidavit notes letter requested August 4, 2017; legal memo states evidence not present at RPD hearing.
propositions.quote: An affidavit in support of the request for the admission of the document merely notes that the document was requested on August 4, 2017 and the Appellant's Legal Memorandum states that the "piece of evidence was not present at the time of the hearing before the RPD".

propositions.text: No argument why German Consulate info was not sought earlier or was unavailable or not reasonably expected to be presented at RPD stage.
propositions.quote: No argument is made as to why the information from the German Consulate was not sought until after the rejection of the claim. Nor does the Appellant indicate why the document was not reasonably available or could not reasonably have been expected to be presented at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant offers no explanation why German Consulate letter was not obtained before RPD rejection or why it was unavailable then.

propositions.text: Fairness requires examining background; Ministry initially sought permission to contact German authorities but later declined to intervene.
propositions.quote: However, in the circumstances, I feel that fairness requires me to look at the background of the issue. The hearing was originally scheduled for May 29, 2017, but was adjourned in order to ensure that the Ministry-which had earlier requested permission from the Appellant to contact the German authorities in relation to a possible Article 1E exclusion-received the signed permission document from the Appellant. The hearing resumed on July 29, 2017; however the Ministry-despite its earlier request-declined to intervene.

propositions.text: Because Ministry initially sought German contact, it was reasonable for appellant not to seek letter earlier; appellant could not reasonably be expected to present letter at RPD stage.
propositions.quote: Because of the Ministry's initial interest in contacting the German authorities, it was reasonable, I find, for the Appellant not to have done so. As such, I find that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the letter from the German consulate at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds fairness requires considering Ministry's initial interest in German contact; appellant reasonably did not seek letter earlier; letter not reasonably expected at RPD stage.

propositions.text: German Consulate letter is credible, new, relevant, and admissible.
propositions.quote: Based on my examination of the document, I can see no basis to find that it is lacking in credibility. It is on letterhead, is signed and appears official. It is clearly new information and it is highly relevant to an essential finding of the RPD: that the Appellant had permanent residency in Germany. Consequently, I find the document admissible.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds German Consulate letter credible, new, relevant, and admits it as evidence.

propositions.text: Appellant offers no argument how affidavit from Mr. XXXX complies with subsection 110(4).
propositions.quote: Once again, the Appellant offers no argument as to how the affidavit from Mr. XXXX XXXX sworn September 25, 2017, complies with subsection 110(4).

propositions.text: Affidavit contains no information that could not have been provided to RPD before claim rejection; affidavit inadmissible.
propositions.quote: It is clear from its content, that it contains no information that could have been either provided to the RPD at the time of the Appellant's hearing or during the period after the last session of the hearing (June 29, 2017) and before the Appellant's claim was rejected (July 14, 2017). As such, I find it inadmissible.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant offers no argument for affidavit's compliance with subsection 110(4); court finds affidavit inadmissible as information was available before RPD rejection.

propositions.text: Appellant requests RAD hearing on new evidence, arguing RPD did not address credibility and affidavit evidence warrants hearing.
propositions.quote: The Appellant is asking to have hearing [sic] before the RAD pursuant to section 110(6) of the IRPA. The RPD did not address issue credibility [sic] as it solely based its decision on exclusion under Article 1A [sic]. There is also new evidence by of Affidavit from Mr. XXXX. The RAD may wish to hear evidence from Mr. XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant requests RAD hearing on new evidence, arguing RPD did not address credibility and affidavit warrants hearing.

propositions.text: Subsection 110(3) IRPA requires RAD to proceed without hearing unless subsection 110(6) conditions met for new evidence hearing.
propositions.quote: The principle under subsection 110(3) of the IRPA that the RAD must proceed without a hearing, is subject to an exception, elaborated in subsection 110(6).

propositions.text: Subsection 110(6) allows hearing if new evidence: a) raises serious credibility issue; b) is central to decision; c) if accepted, justifies allowing or rejecting claim.
propositions.quote: The latter subsection provides a hearing may be held where three conditions in relation to the new evidence are met. The new evidence must: a) raise a serious issue with respect to the Appellant's credibility; b) be central to the decision with respect to his refugee protection claim and c) if accepted, justify allowing or rejecting his claim.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains RAD must proceed without hearing unless subsection 110(6) conditions for new evidence hearing are met.

propositions.text: Affidavit inadmissible; no need to consider subsection 110(6) conditions for hearing on affidavit.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's justification for his request for a hearing centres primarily on the affidavit of Mr. XXXX; given my finding above that his affidavit is inadmissible, I need not have regard to the existence of the three conditions outlined in subsection 110(6) in relation to that affidavit.

propositions.text: Letter from German Consulate admitted but does not justify allowing or rejecting claim; credibility issue remains.
propositions.quote: As to the letter from the German Consulate, I find that the test at section 110(6) is not met: the evidence, though admitted, does not "justify allowing or rejecting his claim." The evidence certainly impacts on the RPD's finding-discussed below-that the Appellant's residence permit in Germany excludes him based on Article 1E; however that alone does not justify allowing or rejecting the Appellant's claim. The issue of his credibility remains.

paragraphs.summary: Court denies hearing request as affidavit inadmissible and German Consulate letter does not justify allowing or rejecting claim; credibility issue remains.

propositions.text: Determinative issues: i) whether appellant is excluded under Article 1E due to German residency; ii) credibility.
propositions.quote: The determinative issues in this case are i) whether the Appellant is disqualified from refugee protection in Canada under Article 1E of the Geneva Convention by virtue of having been recognized as a resident of Germany and ii) credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Court identifies determinative issues as Article 1E exclusion due to German residency and credibility.

propositions.text: Standard of review is correctness except where RPD has meaningful advantage assessing oral testimony, then reasonableness applies.
propositions.quote: The standard of review is correctness,7 except where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment of the oral testimony. If such an advantage exists, I will apply a standard of reasonableness.8 Where I do so, I will so indicate.

paragraphs.summary: Court states standard of review is correctness except when RPD has advantage assessing oral testimony, then reasonableness applies.

propositions.text: RPD found on balance of probabilities that appellant had permanent residence in Germany and lacked credibility due to falsified passport.
propositions.quote: The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant had permanent residence in Germany. It also found that the Appellant lacked credibly as he had submitted a falsified passport when making his refugee claim.

propositions.text: Appellant argues he was not resident of Germany and RPD erred in finding lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that he was not a resident of Germany and that the RPD's finding that he lacked credibility was in error.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found appellant had German residence and lacked credibility; appellant argues he was not resident and RPD erred on credibility.

propositions.text: RPD found Canadian visa officials accepted documents as authentic and appellant had permanent residency in Germany.
propositions.quote: The RPD, noting that the Canadian visa officials had accepted the documents submitted in support of the Appellant's visa application, found that they were, on a balance of probabilities, authentic and found further that he had, as indicated in the visa application, permanent residency in Germany.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found visa officials accepted documents as authentic and appellant had permanent residency in Germany.

propositions.text: Appellant argues documents except passport were forgeries; visa officials may have been fooled but that does not prove genuineness.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues that all of the documents that were a part of his Canadian visa application, other than his passport, were forgeries. He argues that the RPD erred in finding that the Canadian officials who reviewed the visa application would have made a determination that the documentation was genuine; there was no evidence to this effect. Simply because the documentation was realistic enough to fool the visa officials did not mean that it was genuine.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant argues documents except passport were forged; visa officials may have been fooled but that does not prove genuineness.

propositions.text: Admitted German Consulate letter shows residency card was not valid; no indication letter is not authentic.
propositions.quote: As noted, I have admitted into evidence the letter from the German Consulate indicating that the residency card was not valid and I can see no indication that that letter is anything other than authentic.

propositions.text: Important aspect of RPD's finding of permanent residency is missing; court must review RPD's finding on this point.
propositions.quote: As such, an important aspect of the RPD's finding that the Appellant had permanent residency in Germany is missing and I must review its finding on this point.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds German Consulate letter shows residency card invalid, undermining RPD's finding of permanent residency; court must review that finding.

propositions.text: Other documents not found invalid but invalid residency card means court does not share RPD's conclusion appellant was German resident.
propositions.quote: Even though I have no reason to find that the other documents submitted as part of the Appellant's visa application were invalid, because the Residency Card is not valid, I do not share the RPD's conclusion that the Appellant was a German resident.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, appellant did not have permanent residency in Germany; RPD erred in finding exclusion under Article 1E.
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant did not have permanent residency in Germany and that the RPD erred in finding that he was excluded from refugee protection by virtue of Article 1E.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds appellant did not have German permanent residency and RPD erred in Article 1E exclusion finding.

propositions.text: RPD found two versions of appellant's passport; visa application version showed extensive travel; refugee claim version had pages from different passport.
propositions.quote: The RPD reviewed the Appellant's passport and found that there were two versions. In the version that was submitted to the Canadian officials in late 2016 in support of the Appellant's visa application, all pages appeared to be from the same passport and there was evidence of extensive travel on the part of the Appellant. In the second version, the one submitted as part of the Appellant's refugee claim in late March 2017, certain of the passport's pages-in particular the pages that, in the version submitted to the Canadian visa officials, featured stamps showing extensive travel-featured numbers that indicated that they were from a different passport.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found two passport versions: visa application version consistent; refugee claim version had pages from different passport.

propositions.text: RPD suggested two passport versions exist because real passport was modified to hide German connections
propositions.quote: The RPD suggested that the most likely explanation for the existence of two versions of the passport was that the Appellant's real passport was used in the application for a Canadian visa but that after the passport had been returned to the Appellant (with the Canadian visa in it), it had been modified in such a way that the Appellant's connections with Germany would be hidden

propositions.text: Appellant denied knowledge and blamed agent/smuggler for passport fraud
propositions.quote: When confronted with this, the Appellant denied all knowledge attributed any fraud to his agent/smuggler

propositions.text: RPD found photo pages same but visa pages had different numbers in two passport versions
propositions.quote: So we have established that the photo pages that I showed you between the [Canadian visa] application and [the version of the passport submitted in support of the refugee claim] are the same...The visa pages in the [version of the passport submitted in support of the refugee claim] have a different number at the top

propositions.text: RPD rejected Appellant's explanation and found Canadian officials would have noticed tampering
propositions.quote: The RPD rejected this explanation...had it been tampered with at the time of their examination, the officials would not have issued the visa

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found two passport versions, Appellant denied fraud, RPD rejected explanation, found Canadian officials would have noticed tampering.

propositions.text: Appellant claims he provided valid passport to agent/smuggler
propositions.quote: The Appellant claims that he provided a valid passport to the agent/smuggler

propositions.text: Appellant claims he never travelled outside Turkey until coming to Canada
propositions.quote: he claims that he had never travelled outside Turkey until he came to Canada

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD erred in finding Canadian official would have determined documentation genuine
propositions.quote: the Appellant argues that the RPD erred in finding that the Canadian official who reviewed the visa application would have made a determination that the documentation was genuine

propositions.text: Appellant says realistic documentation fooling visa official does not mean it was genuine
propositions.quote: simply because the documentation was realistic enough to fool the visa official, did not mean that it was genuine

paragraphs.summary: Appellant claims valid passport given to smuggler, never travelled outside Turkey, and RPD erred in finding visa official verified genuineness.

propositions.text: Examined two passport versions and confirmed they differ in passport numbers on pages
propositions.quote: I have closely examined the two versions of the Appellant's passport...confirm that the RPD was correct in finding that they were different

propositions.text: Passport number on cover and photo page is XXXX in both versions
propositions.quote: With both versions the passport number is given on the front cover and on the photograph page (page 2) as XXXX

propositions.text: Visa application passport has consistent passport number XXXX on all pages
propositions.quote: the version of the passport that was submitted as part of the application for the Canadian visa has the same passport number, XXXX, stamped on all of the pages provided

propositions.text: Refugee claim passport has inconsistent passport numbers on pages, some XXXX, some XXXX
propositions.quote: the version that was submitted as part of the Appellant's refugee claim does not...pages 1 (the cover) - 3 show the number XXXX; however, on pages 4 - 12 the passport number stamped on the document pages is XXXX

propositions.text: Canadian visa linked to passport number XXXX; number on visa page not legible
propositions.quote: The Canadian visa, found at page 20, is linked to passport number XXXX; the passport number stamped on that page is not legible

paragraphs.summary: Court examined passports, confirmed differences in passport numbers on pages, and noted visa linked to passport number XXXX.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, passport submitted to Canadian visa officials was authentic
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the passport submitted to the Canadian visa officials was authentic

propositions.text: If clumsily modified passport had been submitted, visa officials would have noticed
propositions.quote: Had the clumsily modified version been submitted to the visa officials, they would, on a balance of probabilities, have noticed

propositions.text: Visa officials' role is to ensure visa applications are legitimate
propositions.quote: their role is to ensure that applications for visas are legitimate

paragraphs.summary: Court finds passport submitted to visa officials authentic; officials would have noticed clumsy modifications; their role is to ensure legitimacy.

propositions.text: Version submitted with refugee claim had substituted pages to hide travel evidence
propositions.quote: It is clear that the version submitted in support of the Appellant's refugee claim had substituted pages that corresponded with those pages in the passport submitted as part of the visa application where there was evidence of travel

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, there was an attempt to fraudulently modify passport to hide travel stamps
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that there was an attempt to fraudulently modify the passport so that the travel stamps would not appear in the modified version

paragraphs.summary: Court finds refugee claim passport had substituted pages to hide travel stamps, indicating fraudulent modification attempt.

propositions.text: Appellant says agent/smuggler modified passport after receiving valid passport from him
propositions.quote: it is the position of the Appellant that he gave the agent/smuggler his valid passport and that any substitution of pages was the work of the agent/smuggler

propositions.text: Agent/smuggler would have had to modify passport twice to fool visa officials and then replace pages after visa process
propositions.quote: the agent/smuggler would have not only had to modify the passport with sufficient sophistication to fool Canadian visa officials, he would have also had to replace the pages containing the stamps after it was returned to the agent/smuggler from the Canadian visa officials but before the agent/smuggler returned it to the Appellant

propositions.text: Appellant would have entered Canada with passport showing pages from two different passports, which is implausible
propositions.quote: Such a scenario would mean that the Appellant would have entered Canada on a passport that featured pages stamped as being from two different passports. This is not only implausible

propositions.text: CBSA officials would have noticed altered passport at entry; no advantage to agent/smuggler modifying before travel
propositions.quote: it is also illogical: there would be no advantage to the agent/smuggler modifying the passport before the Appellant travelled and considerable disadvantage

paragraphs.summary: Appellant says smuggler modified passport; court finds double modification implausible and CBSA would have noticed altered passport at entry.

propositions.text: Implausible that clumsily doctored passport would not be spotted by CBSA at airport
propositions.quote: I am of the view that it is implausible that a passport, doctored in the rather clumsy way described, would not have been spotted by the CBSA officials if it had been was presented at Pearson Airport on XXXX XXXX, 2017

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, Appellant travelled to Canada on unaltered passport
propositions.quote: Consequently, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant travelled to Canada on his unaltered passport

paragraphs.summary: Court finds it implausible CBSA missed clumsily doctored passport; concludes Appellant travelled on unaltered passport.

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, passport was tampered with by Appellant after arrival in Canada before refugee claim
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the passport was tampered with by the Appellant (or under his direction) sometime after the Appellant's arrival in Canada and before he surrendered it as part of his refugee claim

propositions.text: Appellant's motives for modifying passport are unknowable but may be to strengthen refugee claim
propositions.quote: he may have thought that removing evidence of foreign travel would strengthen his refugee claim

propositions.text: Fraudulent passport modification seriously undermines Appellant's credibility
propositions.quote: I find that this act of fraud seriously undermines the Appellant's credibility

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Appellant tampered with passport after arrival to strengthen claim; this fraud undermines credibility.

propositions.text: Travel stamps showing extensive travel including Germany are valid
propositions.quote: I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the travel stamps-which show extensive travel, including to Germany-are valid

propositions.text: Appellant's testimony of never leaving Turkey until Canada was fabricated
propositions.quote: his testimony that he had never set foot outside Germany until he came to Canada was a fabrication

propositions.text: Fabrication seriously undermines Appellant's credibility
propositions.quote: I find that this fabrication seriously undermines his credibility

paragraphs.summary: Court finds travel stamps valid, Appellant's testimony fabricated, and fabrication undermines credibility.

propositions.text: Before final credibility finding, court considers supporting documents provided to RPD
propositions.quote: before making a final finding regarding the Appellant's credibility, I turn to the supporting documents provided to the RPD

propositions.text: Appellant submitted Turkish identity card matching name and birth date on passports
propositions.quote: the Appellant has submitted a Turkish identity card showing him to have the same name and date of birth as the person in each version of the passport

propositions.text: Other documents include receipts for HDP and Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association memberships, membership card, letter from Canadian Alevi Culture Centre, and photos
propositions.quote: The only other documents provided by the Appellant are receipts for the payment of membership fees to the HDP, receipts for the payment of membership fees to the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association, a membership card from the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association, a letter from the Canadian Alevi Culture Centre and photographs said to be of the Appellant

paragraphs.summary: Court reviews supporting documents including identity card, membership receipts, letter, and photos before final credibility finding.

propositions.text: Receipts for HDP membership fees appear valid and support Appellant's claim of membership
propositions.quote: The receipts for payment of membership fees to the HDP appear valid on their face and pertain to two years during which the Appellant claims to have been a party member

paragraphs.summary: Court finds HDP membership fee receipts valid and supportive of Appellant's membership claim.

propositions.text: Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association membership fees and card appear valid and support claim of Alevi Muslim identity
propositions.quote: The payments for membership fees and the membership card in the Pir Sultan Abdal Cultural Association appear valid, have probative value and support the Appellant's claim that he was an Alevi Muslim

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Pir Sultan Abdal membership fees and card valid and supportive of Alevi Muslim claim.

propositions.text: Letter from Canadian Alevi Culture Centre states Appellant is Alevi member since March 2017 but unclear how determined
propositions.quote: The letter from the Canadian Alevi Culture Centre, dated April 16, 2017, states that the Appellant is a member of the Alevi faith and had been a member of the community centre since March 2017. I note that the letter does not make clear how the Centre arrived at its finding that he was a member of the Alevi faith

propositions.text: Letter assigned some probative value despite uncertainty
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, I assign the letter some probative value

paragraphs.summary: Court notes letter states Appellant is Alevi member but unclear how determined; assigns some probative value.

propositions.text: Six photos submitted said to be of Appellant; first three show protests with many people, none clearly Appellant
propositions.quote: I have reviewed the photographs and can see no indication that the Appellant features in any of them. The first three pictures said to be taken at protests in Turkey; however, they feature multiple people (as many as 40), none of whom appears to be the Appellant

propositions.text: First three photos assigned no probative value
propositions.quote: I assign these no probative value

propositions.text: Other three photos said to be taken in Canada have limited probative value
propositions.quote: The other three photographs are said to be taken at a time when the Appellant was here in Canada...they are of limited probative value

propositions.text: Participation in Kurdish political events in Canada does not prove participation in Turkey; may be to strengthen false claim
propositions.quote: The fact that he has participated in Kurdish political events while in Canada does not prove that he did so in Turkey. He may well have participated in the events in Canada with a view to strengthening a false refugee claim

paragraphs.summary: Court finds first three photos show no Appellant, no probative value; other three photos limited value; Canadian participation not proof of Turkish activity.

propositions.text: Weighing fraudulent behaviour against documents, Appellant overall lacks credibility
propositions.quote: When I weigh the Appellant's fraudulent behaviour, as outlined above, against to the documents outlined above and their probative value, I find that the Appellant is, overall, lacking in credibility

propositions.text: Claims of persecution by Turkish state on basis of HDP membership are, on balance of probabilities, false
propositions.quote: Consequently, I find that his claims of persecution by the Turkish state on the basis of his membership in the HDP are, on a balance of probabilities, false

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Appellant lacks credibility overall and his persecution claims based on HDP membership are false.

propositions.text: Whether someone similarly situated as Alevi Muslim in Turkey faces serious possibility of persecution or harm under IRPA
propositions.quote: it falls to me to consider whether someone similarly situated as a Alevi Muslim in Turkey would face a serious possibility of persecution or would face, on a balance of probabilities, harm of the nature outlined in subsection 97(1) of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: Court considers if similarly situated Alevi Muslim in Turkey faces serious persecution or harm under IRPA.

propositions.text: Reviewed documents submitted by Appellant and National Documentation Package
propositions.quote: I have reviewed documents submitted by the Appellant before the RPD, only two of which touch on the situation of Alevi Muslims in Turkey, as well as the National Documentation Package

propositions.text: Two articles submitted by Appellant are of limited value and not relevant to 2018 situation
propositions.quote: The two articles submitted by the Appellant before the RPD are of limited value: the first deals with an incident from 1993 and is not relevant to the situation in 2018 and the second makes only passing reference to a single incident involving an attack against Alevi neighbourhoods during the attempted coup in 2016

paragraphs.summary: Court reviewed documents and found two articles submitted by Appellant limited and not relevant to 2018.

propositions.text: Alevi Muslims in Turkey face inequalities including lack of official recognition of worship places and religious instruction issues
propositions.quote: It is clear from the objective evidence that the 15 - 20 million Alevi Muslims in Turkey face inequalities. These include not having their places of worship officially recognized...difficulties establishing new places of worship...refusal to allow Alevi children an exemption from compulsory Sunni Islamic instruction

propositions.text: Small number of reports of ill-treatment by authorities mainly during demonstrations
propositions.quote: There have also been a small number of reports of ill-treatment of Alevis by the authorities, primarily in the context of demonstrations by the Alevi community

propositions.text: Isolated incidents of societal discrimination and violence reported but most Alevis coexist peacefully
propositions.quote: Isolated incidents of societal discrimination and violence towards Alevis have been reported but "these are few and most Alevis co-exist with other communities with few problems on a daily basis

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Alevi Muslims face inequalities and some ill-treatment but mostly coexist peacefully in Turkey.

propositions.text: UK Home Office summary: treatment of Alevis does not amount to persecution or serious harm
propositions.quote: Even when taken cumulatively, the treatment faced by Alevis does not in general amount to them being subject to action on the part of either non-state actors or the authorities which would amount to persecution or serious harm

propositions.text: Court agrees with UK Home Office summary that Alevis do not face serious possibility of persecution in Turkey
propositions.quote: I agree with this summary. I find that, despite the existence of problems, Alevi Muslims in general do not face a serious possibility of persecution in Turkey

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees with UK Home Office that Alevis do not face serious persecution in Turkey despite problems.

propositions.text: Appellant will not face serious possibility of persecution on return to Turkey
propositions.quote: I find the Appellant will not face a serious possibility of persecution on his return to Turkey

propositions.text: On balance of probabilities, Appellant will not face harm under subsection 97(1) of IRPA
propositions.quote: I find further that, on a balance of probabilities, he will not face harm of the nature described in subsection 97(1) of the IRPA

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Appellant will not face serious persecution or harm under IRPA on return to Turkey.

propositions.text: The Appeal is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The Appeal is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal.
